slides.title: Four words, no account
slides.subtitle: One secret that names you, draws your card, and carries your saves between screens. No email. No password. No sign-in.
slides.notes: Say it plainly: the account IS the four words. Nothing else is issued, and nothing else is stored to identify you. Slide 6 is the system on one plate; slide 8 is the real cards.

slides.headline: Every other tool puts a doorman in front of the door
body: To save a thing, the usual stack asks for: an email address, a password, a code sent to a phone, a row in someone's Postgres, and a "forgot password" flow for the day you lose the lot.
None of that is the interesting part of a tool. It is the toll booth you pay to be remembered.

body.title: The interesting question
body.body: How much identity do you actually need in order to be remembered on a second screen? Less than we've been sold.

slides.headline: One secret, short enough to say across a room
body: Four words, drawn from a curated bank of **4,096**. That is **48 bits**: 281,474,976,710,656 combinations.
Words, not a hex string, because a passphrase gets *said* — across a couch, down a phone, onto a TV remote — and still survives being remembered a week later.

body.title: Why 48 bits is plenty here
body.body: Nothing is guessing this over HTTP. The realistic failure is a person copying it somewhere careless — which is why rotation matters more than stretching.

slides.headline: The words become a handle you can print
body: `HMAC("softstack-passport-code:" + phrase, secret)` → twelve hex characters → **`SS-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX`**.
One-way on purpose: the code is public (it is printed on the card), and a code alone never walks you back to the words.
Every app that reads a card can verify the handle without ever holding the phrase.

slides.headline: The handle becomes a person, on your device
body: `SHA-256("softstack-passport-id:" + code)` seeds all of it: your moniker *(adjective + animal)*, a DiceBear face, a palette, a foil, a frame.
All of it is computed **before any network call**. That is not a detail — it is the feature: mistype a word and the wrong animal appears *instantly*, so the card debugs the copy.
Identity is minted once and kept, so expanding the word bank later can never rename someone who already exists.

image.alt: Diagram: four words become an SS- code by HMAC; the code becomes an identity and card by SHA-256; the same words derive the vault folder by SHA-256; any other screen resumes with #phrase=

slides.headline: Eight palettes, five axes, 7,680 cards
body: Palettes: **Sunset · Miami · Lavender · Pool · Risograph · Mango · Grape Soda · Spearmint**. Times 4 foils, 4 frames, 5 textures, 3 type styles and 4 avatar sets = **7,680 cards**, all derived from the same four words, offline.

slides.headline: Twelve of the 7,680, drawn from twelve phrases

image.alt: Twelve passport cards from twelve passphrases, each labelled with its palette, foil, frame, texture and type

slides.notes: Every tile is a real card: seven palettes, all four foils, all four frames, all five textures, three type styles and all four avatar sets. Not one request to a server to draw any of them. The point of this slide is coverage, not beauty: the axes are all represented.

slides.headline: The card is a licence, and it has two sides

left.headline: Front — who you are
body: The moniker, the face, and the four words held behind dots with a REVEAL.
A gold chip and a foil seal because a document should feel like a document.
Nothing on the front is a secret that unlocks anything.

right.headline: Back — how to carry it
body: A scannable code, a serial, a magnetic stripe.
Tap the card and it turns over; the four words own the whole front row instead of sharing it with a stamp.
The flip exists so the code can be big enough to actually scan.

slides.headline: The QR is the words, in a box
body: It encodes `https://…/arcade/#phrase=<the four words>`. Scanning it and typing them into **4 WORDS** are the same act.
The `#` is doing real work: fragments are never sent to a server, never logged, never in a referrer.
That is also why the QR is *not* a second credential — there is nothing in it but the words.

slides.headline: Where it lands: a folder, not an account
body: `~/arcade-saves/` + `sha256(four words)[:32]` → one small JSON per game, per kind: a **save state** and a **battery save**.
`{ game, kind, data, timestamp }`. The index is the same shape with `hasState` / `hasSram` flags.
One slot each. Whoever writes last wins — there is no history and no conflict prompt.

slides.headline: The round trip, as it was actually tested
body: Phone saves → `POST /api/arcade/save` **200**.
A cold laptop with nothing in storage opens the link → the passport reads **`passport · 1`**, one game saved.
**RESUME** → `GET` **200** → the state applies and the game continues where the phone left it.

body.title: That is the whole trick
body.body: No sign-in screen appears anywhere in that story. The four words were the entire hand-off.

left.headline: What linking does
body: Scan someone's QR (or type their words) and your device *adopts* that secret.
Both devices now read and write the same folder. That is what "sync" means here.

right.headline: What never happens
body: Two different secrets are two different folders. They do not merge, and nothing reconciles them.
Adopting new words forgets the old ones locally — note them first, or that vault is stranded until you type them again.

slides.headline: Encrypted in transit. Not yet at rest.
body: TLS between the browser and the box. The folder name is the hash of the words. The blobs inside are plaintext JSON.
Anyone who can read the disk can read the saves. So can the box's owner — which is the point of a home server, but worth saying out loud.
The upgrade is client-side AES-GCM with a separate lookup id, plus an upgrade-on-read migration. Planned, not shipped.

body.title: Don't oversell this
body.body: It is game saves and notes. The threat that actually bites is you pasting the four words somewhere careless.

slides.headline: Unhook is local. Revocation is new words.

left.headline: Disconnect this device
body: Two taps. Clears the passphrase, the callsign and this browser's local save stores, then reloads into a fresh passport.
The vault is untouched: a seeded save still answered 200 afterwards. Verified, not assumed.

right.headline: New words
body: Minting a new phrase is the only real revocation, because there is no account to disable.
The old vault stays behind, readable by anyone still holding the old four words. That is the trade for having no accounts.

slides.headline: Five surfaces, one source of truth
body: One canonical module: the word bank, the derivation, the palettes, the card. TalkType, ZipList, QRBuddy and ProMapper vendor it **byte-for-byte** and check it in CI.
Four of them also sign an HS256 token carrying `stamps` and `tier` — the thing that unlocks a paid feature.
The arcade is the fifth stamp, and it is honest about being a fork: it keeps the shared card plus its own sheet CSS, and it skips the token entirely because there is nothing to unlock.

slides.headline: What it can't do
body: **No merge.** Two secrets are two vaults; combining them is a project, not a button.
**No recovery.** Lose all four words with no device holding them and the saves are gone. No email falls back.
**Last write wins.** Two screens saving the same game keep the later timestamp, silently.
**No backup yet.** The vault is one folder on one disk. That is the next piece of work.
**Contrast varies.** A couple of palettes put pale ink on pale gradients; the card is derived, not art-directed per person.

slides.headline: Minting a passport takes about ten seconds
body: Open the arcade, tap **passport**, read the four words. That is the account — there is nothing else to fill in.
Copy the link or scan the card on the next screen. Save the words somewhere you can find them, because nobody else can.
Play something. Save. Open the arcade on another device and put the same four words in.

slides.quote: "The four words are the key, the name, and the portrait — and the only thing you have to remember."
